textbookText: Derived Quantities These are the quantities that are derived from the fundamental quantities. Examples: velocity, momentum, force, pressure, etc. disp lacem ent Velocity = time And momentum = mass × velocity = mass × displacement time Here, the two derived quantities were obtained from different fundamental quantities simply by dividing or multiplying them. 1.3 Measurement and its need In the past, especially at the time of Aristotle, the observations on natural science were subjective and the observations varied from one to another because they depended on one’s senses. This made communication among physicists difficult. For the description of a physical quantity, it should have the system of measurement as per Lord Kelvin (1824 – 1907), any measurement should be expressed in numerical value for a complete sense. Hence otherwise it has no place in physics. An unknown quantity if compared to a known reference value is called measurement in physics. The known reference value is called the unit. Why do we need measurement? i) To test the concepts in our hypothesis, we need measurement. The measured concepts finally become the variables.

ii) To understand the phenomenon in physics, one has to perform the experiments. The experiments require measurement and one measures several physical properties like length, mass, time, temperature, etc iii) For the experimental verification of laws and theories, one needs the measurement of physical properties.

Concept of measurement: Assigning the numerical values to the physical quantities by comparing them with their respective units is measurement. 1.4 Unit of a Physical Quantity As mentioned earlier, a physical quantity should have a system of measurement; it should be measured and expressed in numbers. The standard of measurement of reference is the unit.
Conventions in Writing a Unit: i) For the unit that is named after a scientist, write the first letter as small letter instead of a capital letter.

For example, we write newton butnot Newton. Similarly, it is written joule but not Joule. ii) If the unit named after a person is to be written as a symbol, we use a capital letter whereas the symbols for other units not fromed from a person's name aren’t written in capital letters. For example, N for newton (not n) and m for meter (not M). iii) The symbols of units are never expressed in the plural form. We use 5 erg (and not 5 ergs), 5 kilo (and not 5 kilos), 10 m (but not 10 ms). iv) For the symbols of the derived unit, multiplication is joined with a centre dot or a non-brake space as N.m or Nm v) For the units of derived quantities, the symbols obtained after division are joined using solidus or as a negative exponent. For example, metre per second is written as either ms-1 or ms-1. The solidus is used only as one i.e., kg/ms-2 and not as kg/ms-1 -2.

However, kgm-1s2 can also be written in place of kg/ms-2. vi) Symbols must be treated as mathematical entities but not as abbreviations, and they do not have an appended period and full stop. vii) Full stops aren’t written after the abbreviated units. For example, 50cc 50 ml, but not 50 c.c and 50 m. l.
viii) Names of units are pluralized i.e., henries and not henry. Lux, hertz, and siemens are the exceptional cases.
Since a prefix is a part of unit, it is prepended to the unit symbol without a separator.

Examples: G in GHz, M in MPa, and k in km. ix) Units are of two types; Fundamental unit and derived unit. x) 1.4.1 Fundamental and Derived Units The units involved in the measurement of fundamental physical quantities are the fundamental units.
The units involved in the measurements of derived physical quantities are the derived units.

The derived units are brought from the fundamental units by simply multiplying or dividing two or more fundamental units. 1.4.2 System of Units At different times in history, and in different parts of the world, people used different sets of units for measurement. The commonly used systems of units are MKS, CGS and FPS. The internationally accepted system of units used in science and engineering is called the SI unit.
MKS system: In this system of measurement, length is measured in metre, mass is measured in kilogram, and time is measured in second. It was developed in France.
CGS System: In it, length is measured in centimeter, mass in gram and the time is measured in second. This system was also developed in France.
FPS System: In it, length is measured in foot, mass in pound and the time is measured in second. It was developed in Britain and is known as British system of units.

SI Units: In 1960, to bring uniformity in measurement in the worldwide sense, the convention of scientists held in Paris introduced units based on scientific facts, and is now accepted internationally. This system of units is called SI unit which stands for the Système international d'unités in the French language.
